source: Google Drive, account the project owner
note: Aokigahara research documents held in the project owner’s Drive, pulled in so the written research travels with the reconstruction. Each file is byte-identical to its Drive original and records the Drive file id, so the source is always locatable. A .txt extraction sits beside each PDF for searching and diffing.

classifications.project-research: Research generated for this project. Historical and cultural, not geospatial: it constrains meaning and context rather than geometry.
classifications.third-party-academic: Published academic work by others. Reference only; copyright is not the project’s to grant.

notInDrive: No geospatial data was found: no shapefiles, GeoJSON, DEM tiles or GPX. The GSI elevation grids, Ministry of the Environment land-cover masks and Geological Survey of Japan Jōgan masks the runtime uses were already ingested and live in viewer/assets/terrain/. What is still missing is the GSJ 2016 vector geology that would replace the raster-derived Jōgan mask, and that is not held in Drive.

notIngested.reason: Provenance and licence unknown. This project tracks the licence of every visual source, so it is recorded rather than committed.

files.note: Century-by-century historical research, 7th to 19th century. 101 pages. Project research output.

Modern period: first half of the 20th century, second half, and the 21st. 40 pages. Project research output. Also present in Drive as document_pdf.pdf (1A4hv1zEj1U9nRJ3qtwq9UDz8Byabl3ab), byte-identical.
Twelfth century only. Matsudai Shonin, Dainichi-ji at the summit in 1149, Fuji as an ascetic Buddhist mountain.
Thirteenth century only. The 1203 Hitoana cave exploration in Azuma Kagami; Fuji lava caves as underworld thresholds.
Fourteenth century only. Lay ascent, oshi and shukubo, the Yoshida route, the 1384 Subashiri kakebotoke.
Fifteenth century only. Murayama Shugendo, Doko’s 1486 Kaikoku Zakki, the Fuji Mandala tradition.

Kathryn Yalan Chang, "A Perfect Place to Die": Thinking the EcoGothic, Darkness, and the Dark Sweet in Gus Van Sant’s The Sea of Trees. SARE vol. 59 issue 1, 2022. Third-party academic work, included for reference; copyright remains with its author and publisher.
